ocar.opportunity: Connectomics usually reverse-engineers existing brains: observe the wiring, take it apart, and infer how it works. Synthetic biology instead builds living systems from parts, on the idea that construction is a powerful way to understand function.
ocar.challenge: Those two traditions have grown separately. There is no established program for artificially designing and assembling the connectomes of live, behaving organisms, or for using such constructs to test theories of network function.
ocar.action: I. Rabinowitch, in Physics of Life Reviews (2020), reviews the idea of synthetic connectomics as a meeting point of connectomics and synthetic biology.
ocar.resolution: The review asks what a synthetic connectome would look like, what it would be for, and how it might be built. Rabinowitch argues it could unify questions about brain operation, perhaps generate new forms of artificial life, and give an empirical way to test theoretical predictions about networks.
ocar.future_work: The piece frames itself as laying out initial steps toward implementation and as contemplating scientific and social impact, not as a completed construction method.

summaries.beginner: Most brain-mapping work takes existing wiring apart. This essay asks what it would mean to build a living wiring diagram from parts, the way synthetic biologists build new cells, and what that might teach us.
summaries.intermediate: In Physics of Life Reviews (2020), I. Rabinowitch proposes synthetic connectomics: artificially designing and constructing connectomes in live behaving organisms. The review contrasts reverse-engineering traditions in biology with construction-based synthetic biology and sketches purposes, possible construction routes, and broader scientific and societal implications. It is a conceptual review, not a methods paper with a built synthetic nervous system.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not specify organisms, parts lists, or experimental results. Claims about unifying brain theory or generating artificial life are programmatic. Do not treat this card as evidence that a synthetic connectome has been built.

plain_language_summary: Most brain-mapping work takes existing wiring apart. This essay asks what it would mean to build a living wiring diagram from parts, the way synthetic biologists build new cells, and what that might teach us.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomics is still too slow to map entire mammalian brains. Expansion microscopy raises effective resolution linearly but enlarges tissue cubically, so imaging time explodes. Fast X-ray tomography could offset that volume penalty if expanded tissue could be stained for X-rays.
ocar.challenge: No group had imaged cellular features inside expanded tissue with X-ray microscopy. Expanded gels have gaps that fluorescence can fill but X-rays cannot, and laboratory X-ray microscopes differ from the synchrotron instruments that would actually be fast enough for large volumes.
ocar.action: Logan Thrasher Collins reports on arXiv (2026) a first demonstration of expansion X-ray microscopy (ExXRM): an ~18× expanded mouse cortex prepared with pan-ExM, enzymatic Unclearing with diaminobenzidine deposition, metallic gold enhancement, and imaging on a laboratory X-ray microscope.
ocar.resolution: Cell bodies were reconstructable in the expanded volume—the first time, the author states, that biological features of any kind were imaged with X-ray microscopy in expanded tissue. Visibility came largely as negative space: cytosol stained less than surrounding tissue. Neurites were not resolved because of extensive off-target staining.
ocar.future_work: The discussion calls next for metallic amplification with much better on-target staining so dendrites and axons appear, then better stain penetration (the GoldEnhance kit reached only a few hundred micrometers), then cryopreservation and related tricks so the method can move from laboratory X-ray microscopy to synchrotron beams.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps at synapse scale are still too slow for whole mammalian brains. This early report stains expanded mouse cortex with gold and shows cell bodies on a lab X-ray microscope, a first step toward faster X-ray connectomics after tissue expansion.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2026), Logan Thrasher Collins combines pan-ExM of mouse cortex (~18× expansion) with enzymatic Unclearing, DAB deposition, and GoldEnhance gold staining, then images the gel on a laboratory X-ray microscope. The paper reports the first reconstruction of cell bodies in expanded tissue by X-ray microscopy. Fine neurites are not resolved; the author attributes that to off-target stain. Theoretical motivation is that 0.3 µm X-ray voxels could become ~30 nm or ~15 nm effective voxels at 10× or 20× expansion, with X-ray speed offsetting the cubic volume increase.
summaries.advanced: This is an early-stage methods note, not a connectomic reconstruction. Only cell bodies are shown, via a negative-space staining effect, not axons, dendrites, or synapses. Imaging is laboratory X-ray microscopy, not synchrotron tomography; the author stresses that gold stains, bubble formation in hydrated gels, and heat from metal absorption are unproven at synchrotron dose. Diffusion depth of the gold kit is limited to a few hundred micrometers of expanded tissue. Catalog organism tags saying “other” should not override the mouse-cortex sample in the PDF.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps at synapse scale are still too slow for whole mammalian brains. This early report stains expanded mouse cortex with gold and shows cell bodies on a lab X-ray microscope, a first step toward faster X-ray connectomics after tissue expansion.

ocar.opportunity: How a circuit’s detailed wiring shapes behavior is a core question. In C. elegans the nociceptive circuit uses the same neurons in both sexes but wires them differently, offering a natural test of topology versus cell identity.
ocar.challenge: Nociceptive sensory neurons respond similarly in the two sexes, yet the animals show sexually dimorphic avoidance. That leaves downstream network topology as a candidate explanation that is hard to isolate without targeted rewiring.
ocar.action: Pechuk, Goldman, Oren-Suissa and colleagues, catalogued as Current Biology (2022), learn and simulate network models of the dimorphic behaviors, predict simple synaptic rewirings that should switch sex-typical responses, and test those rewirings experimentally.
ocar.resolution: The predicted subtle rewirings flip behavior between the sexes. Rewired males were worse at finding mating partners when aversive cues were present, which the authors read as a reproductive cost of topologies that avoid noxious cues efficiently.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the work as a deconstruction of how a sexual-behavior circuit is designed and how it can be reprogrammed; further circuits and costs are not specified here.

summaries.beginner: Male and female roundworms use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, and they behave differently toward the same nasty smells. This team predicts tiny wiring swaps that should flip those behaviors—and then makes those swaps and watches the animals change.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Pechuk, Goldman, Salzberg, Portman, Ferkey, Schneidman, Oren-Suissa and colleagues study the C. elegans nociceptive circuit. Sensory responses are similar across sexes, but avoidance is dimorphic. Network models that reproduce the two behaviors predict simple rewirings that should switch sex-typical output; experiments confirm that those rewirings flip behavior. Rewired males were compromised in finding mating partners in the presence of aversive cues, suggesting a reproductive cost of efficient nociceptive avoidance.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not give synapse counts, which exact synapses were moved, stimulus identities, or sample sizes. “Flip behavior” is qualitative. The SSRN-style DOI in the catalog is a preprint identifier even though the venue is listed as Current Biology; this card does not resolve version-of-record pagination.

plain_language_summary: Male and female roundworms use the same pain-sensing cells but wire them differently, and they behave differently toward the same nasty smells. This team predicts tiny wiring swaps that should flip those behaviors—and then makes those swaps and watches the animals change.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous systems can be treated as multiscale networks whose communities capture densely linked groups of cells. Those communities may hide still-smaller integrator units that current clustering misses.
ocar.challenge: Standard community detection does not isolate local integrator units (LUs): connected subnetworks whose connections stay inside the unit, as a set of interneurons might. Sensitivity to algorithm choice and network parameters is also unclear.
ocar.action: Shi, Levina, and Noori, in Physical Review E (2019), detect communities with Louvain clustering, use participation coefficients to separate local neurons from global hubs, and search for LUs. They test the scheme on synthetic networks and on weighted and binary C. elegans connectomes.
ocar.resolution: In the worm, detected LUs are distinctly localized along the body and line up with functional groups. Simulations probe how community algorithm and network parameters affect LU recovery. The authors offer the method as an observer-independent parcellation for architecture and functional-connectivity analysis.
ocar.future_work: The abstract positions the approach as useful for confirming functional structure and for quantitative whole-brain architectonics across species; those extensions are not demonstrated here beyond C. elegans.

summaries.beginner: Brain networks are often chopped into communities of tightly linked cells, but smaller local teams can hide inside those communities. This paper’s algorithm looks for those local teams in the worm’s wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review E (2019), Shi, Levina, and Noori define local integrator units as internally connected subnetworks and find them by combining Louvain communities with participation coefficients that flag global hubs. Sensitivity is tested on synthetic graphs. On weighted and binary C. elegans connectomes, LUs are spatially localized in the worm body and match functional groups. The paper offers this as a refined, observer-independent parcellation.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No counts of LUs, no modularity scores, and no named neuron lists appear in the abstract. “Clearly define functional groups” is not accompanied by a behavior or physiology assay here. Results are for C. elegans connectomes, not a new EM reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Brain networks are often chopped into communities of tightly linked cells, but smaller local teams can hide inside those communities. This paper’s algorithm looks for those local teams in the worm’s wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing connectomes across species could reveal which wiring motifs are general and which are species-specific, linking network architecture to cognition and behavior.
ocar.challenge: Cross-species quantitative comparison of brain-network topology was not yet framed as a named program with conserved themes and a space of allowed variation.
ocar.action: M. P. van den Heuvel, E. Bullmore, and O. Sporns introduce comparative connectomics in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2016), surveying connectomes from simple to more advanced species.
ocar.resolution: They identify two conserved wiring themes: community structure serving specialized function, and investment in short paths, hubs, and rich clubs for topological integration. Within that shared space, they argue that differences between closely related species support adaptations in cognition and behavior.
ocar.future_work: The review aims at discovering general principles and species-specific features; it does not itself deliver a new multi-species dataset.

summaries.beginner: Brains of different animals are wired differently, but some patterns may be shared. This review compares those wiring diagrams and argues that communities plus a few well-connected hubs show up again and again.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2016), van den Heuvel, Bullmore, and Sporns define comparative connectomics as quantitative study of cross-species commonalities and variation in brain-network topology. Comparing simple to more advanced species, they highlight conserved community organization and a drive toward integration via short paths, hubs, and rich clubs. Differences among close relatives are interpreted as cognitive and behavioral adaptations within those constraints.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a review, not a new connectome. The abstract names no species list, no graph metrics, and no statistical tests. “Simple to more advanced” is the authors’ framing and should not be read as a ranked scala naturae with numbers attached.

plain_language_summary: Brains of different animals are wired differently, but some patterns may be shared. This review compares those wiring diagrams and argues that communities plus a few well-connected hubs show up again and again.

ocar.opportunity: Large EM and X-ray microtomography volumes can show cells and synapses, but they are useful to others only if annotations travel across tools. FAIR standards would let labs query, share, and reuse costly petascale reconstructions.
ocar.challenge: Without common annotation standards, datasets risk sitting unused as they grow past petascale. Existing pipelines differ in how they name neuronal entities, biological parts, and metadata, and community tools are only partly aligned.
ocar.action: Guittari, Wimbish, Rivlin, Gray-Roncal and colleagues, on arXiv (2024), outline a nanoscale connectomics annotation standards framework with a global BENCHMARK working group of academic and industry partners. They propose building on community platforms such as CAVE, NeuPrint, Neuroglancer, NEURD, and NeuVue, and expanding CAVE schemas (for example BoundSpatialPoint) with BENCHMARK-defined classes.
ocar.resolution: The preprint is a framework and community process, not a finished standard dump. It argues for schematized yet adaptable annotations, versioned community outlines, and CAVE-centered metadata so spatial annotations stay linked to segments. The goal is interoperability across species and modalities.
ocar.future_work: The authors describe ongoing CAVE schema expansion, community critique, and further alignment of EM and XRM pipelines; those remain in-progress working-group tasks in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make and hard to share if every lab labels cells differently. This group sketches common annotation rules so those maps can be found, compared, and reused.
summaries.intermediate: In an October 2024 arXiv preprint, Guittari, Wimbish, Rivlin, Hinton, Matelsky, Wester, Johnson, Gray-Roncal and colleagues (Johns Hopkins APL, with a listed BENCHMARK working group) propose FAIR annotation standards for EM and X-ray microtomography connectomics. They review gaps in current pipelines and argue for embracing existing community software (CAVE, NeuPrint, Neuroglancer, NEURD, NeuVue) while extending CAVE schemas with additional spatial and functional annotation classes. The paper is a standards-framework outline and community agenda rather than a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint on annotation policy and tooling, not a connectome or a benchmark accuracy paper. Schema expansion is described as underway (“actively working with CAVE schemas”), so the extract does not freeze a complete released ontology. Tool mentions are adoption targets, not performance comparisons. No dataset sizes, species reconstructions, or inter-annotator metrics are reported here.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope and X-ray brain maps are expensive to make and hard to share if every lab labels cells differently. This group sketches common annotation rules so those maps can be found, compared, and reused.

ocar.opportunity: Topographic maps order neurons by tuning across species. In Drosophila, lobula columnar (LC) types each form a glomerulus in a stereotyped central-brain position, which might help downstream cells combine visual features.
ocar.challenge: Why those glomeruli sit where they do, and whether neighbors share related selectivities, was unclear from anatomy alone.
ocar.action: Klapoetke, Nern, Rogers, Rubin, Reiser, and Card, in Neuron (2022), record 10 glomeruli with single-neuron calcium imaging and compare the functional map with connectome wiring of downstream neurons.
ocar.resolution: They report new detectors for objects smaller than the lens resolution (LC18) and for complex line motion (LC25). Glomeruli cluster by looming versus drifting object motion and are ordered by size tuning, forming a topographic visual-feature map. Downstream neurons integrate sparse subsets of glomeruli, biased toward similar features.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents LC neurons as an explicit example of feature detectors arranged to ease downstream integration; further types beyond the 10 glomeruli are not covered here.

summaries.beginner: In the fruit fly, some visual cells dump their signals into little knots (glomeruli) in a fixed layout. This paper shows that neighbors in that layout care about similar things, like looming versus sliding objects, which may help the next cells combine those messages.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2022), Klapoetke, Nern, Rogers, Rubin, Reiser, and Card image ten Drosophila lobula-columnar glomeruli one neuron at a time. They identify LC18 as a detector of objects smaller than ommatidial resolution and LC25 as a complex line-motion detector. Glomeruli are spatially clustered by looming versus drifting selectivity and ordered by size tuning. Connectome analysis shows downstream neurons sample sparse, feature-similar glomerulus combinations rather than arbitrary mixes.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Only ten glomeruli are discussed. Tuning claims are qualitative in the abstract (no curves, n, or statistics). “Smaller than the lens resolution” is the authors’ phrasing for LC18, not a measured acuity number here. Downstream sparsity is not quantified as a fraction of possible combinations.

plain_language_summary: In the fruit fly, some visual cells dump their signals into little knots (glomeruli) in a fixed layout. This paper shows that neighbors in that layout care about similar things, like looming versus sliding objects, which may help the next cells combine those messages.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM can show synapses and mitochondria in 3D, but full-volume reconstruction is computationally heavy. Targeted reconstruction of those organelles can still inform structural plasticity.
ocar.challenge: Identifying synapses and mitochondria across large ssEM stacks by hand is impractical, and linking their ultrastructure to learning remains hard.
ocar.action: Liu, Qi, Chen, Xie, Han, Yang and colleagues, in Cell Reports (2022), apply a Region-CNN deep-learning method to segment synapses and mitochondria in mouse auditory cortex after fear conditioning.
ocar.resolution: After reconstructing over 135,000 mitochondria and 160,000 synapses, they report that fear conditioning increases mitochondrial number but decreases mitochondrial size, and promotes multi-contact synapses (one bouton onto multiple postsynaptic sites from different dendrites). Modeling indicates that configuration raises information-storage capacity of new synapses by over 50%.
ocar.future_work: The abstract highlights speed and accuracy of the reconstruction method as a route to cellular plasticity in fear learning; broader behaviors or regions are not tested here.

summaries.beginner: Fear learning may change tiny parts of brain cells, not just whole circuits. This team trains a computer to find synapses and mitochondria in electron-microscope stacks from mice that learned a fear association.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell Reports (2022), Liu, Qi, Chen, Li, Hong, Ma, Shen, Kong, Zhai, Xie, Han, Yang and colleagues use a Region-CNN to identify synapses and mitochondria in ssEM of mouse auditory cortex after fear conditioning. They reconstruct more than 135,000 mitochondria and 160,000 synapses. Fear conditioning is reported to increase mitochondrial number, decrease mitochondrial size, and promote multi-contact synapses. A model claims that geometry raises information-storage capacity of new synapses by over 50%.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Control versus conditioned group sizes, reconstruction accuracy, and the storage-capacity model’s assumptions are not in the abstract. “Over 50%” is a modeling result, not a measured memory improvement. The work is targeted organelle reconstruction, not a full circuit connectome of auditory cortex.

plain_language_summary: Fear learning may change tiny parts of brain cells, not just whole circuits. This team trains a computer to find synapses and mitochondria in electron-microscope stacks from mice that learned a fear association.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva has about 10,000 neurons, genetic tools, solid learning assays, single-cell manipulations, and an emerging complete CNS connectome, making it a tractable memory system.
ocar.challenge: Even the well-studied insect mushroom body still hid more than half of its connection classes until a connectome was available, so circuit-level accounts of larval memory were incomplete.
ocar.action: Thum and Gerber review larval mushroom-body connectomics and function in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019).
ocar.resolution: The connectome revealed circuitry that mixes higher-order sensory input, valence signals, and output neurons that instruct behavior, including cross-hemisphere integration. Activating individual dopaminergic mushroom-body input neurons can reward or punish an odor depending on relative timing. Larvae form molecularly dissociable short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the larval mushroom body as a study case for a nuanced account of molecular function in a behaviorally meaningful memory network.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae have a small memory center that scientists can map synapse by synapse. This review explains how that wiring, plus timing of dopamine signals, helps the larva learn what to approach or avoid.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Andreas S. Thum and B. Gerber review the Drosophila larval mushroom body. They note that the connectome showed more than half of connection classes had been missed, and that the circuit integrates sensory, valence, and output pathways within and across hemispheres. Dopaminergic input-neuron activation can be rewarding or punishing depending on timing relative to odor. Larvae form molecularly dissociable short-term, long-term, and amnesia-resistant memories.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a review of an emerging larval connectome, not a new full-CNS reconstruction in this paper. “More than half of the classes of connection” is a qualitative census from the reviewed connectome work, without a table here. Memory-type dissociations are cited, not re-demonstrated with methods in this abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae have a small memory center that scientists can map synapse by synapse. This review explains how that wiring, plus timing of dopamine signals, helps the larva learn what to approach or avoid.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can show membranes and small vesicles over cellular fields of view, which matters for connectomics as well as cell and matrix biology.
ocar.challenge: Large-scale 3D ultrastructure on a cellular scale was historically limited by how hard serial-section TEM and related methods were to run at throughput.
ocar.action: Smith and Starborg review serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBFSEM) in Tissue & Cell (2019), covering the 2004-developed method from a technical standpoint, with emphasis on cellular applications and later image analysis.
ocar.resolution: They present SBFSEM as having increased reliability, availability, and throughput of 3DEM, with resolution sufficient for membranes and small vesicles and a large field of view, and as a major tool across connectomics and cell biology since its introduction.
ocar.future_work: The review points to subsequent image-analysis techniques as part of the SBFSEM workflow; it does not introduce a new instrument.

summaries.beginner: Taking thousands of electron-microscope slices by hand is slow and finicky. This review explains a scanner that shaves and images a block of tissue automatically so researchers can see cells in 3D.
summaries.intermediate: In Tissue & Cell (2019), David J. Smith and T. Starborg review serial block-face SEM, developed in 2004, as a volume-EM method that improved reliability and throughput relative to classical serial-section TEM and electron tomography. They discuss technical aspects, cellular applications including connectomics, and downstream image analysis. The abstract claims membrane-and-vesicle resolution with large fields of view.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a methods review, not a new connectome. No voxel sizes, volumes, or species reconstructions are given in the abstract. “Developed in 2004” refers to the technique’s origin, not a result of this paper.

plain_language_summary: Taking thousands of electron-microscope slices by hand is slow and finicky. This review explains a scanner that shaves and images a block of tissue automatically so researchers can see cells in 3D.

ocar.opportunity: Brain disease rarely stays in one place; it often spreads along axonal pathways. The connectome’s organized topology therefore constrains how pathology propagates and how the brain adapts.
ocar.challenge: Locus-centric accounts miss network-level maladaptation (diaschisis, transneuronal degeneration, dedifferentiation) and the resources that support compensation (degeneracy, reserve).
ocar.action: Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear review connectomic approaches to neuropathology in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015).
ocar.resolution: They argue that network organization fundamentally shapes responses to damage and that a network-science connectomic approach is integral to understanding neuropathology. Knowledge of topology can move from description to predictive models of spread and functional consequences.
ocar.future_work: The review’s implied program is generating predictive models of disease spread and functional impact from network topology.

summaries.beginner: Brain diseases often travel along the brain’s existing roads rather than staying in one neighborhood. This review explains how mapping those roads can help predict where damage will spread and how the brain copes.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015), Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear review how connectome topology shapes neural responses to damage. They highlight maladaptive processes (diaschisis, transneuronal degeneration, dedifferentiation) and adaptive resources (degeneracy, reserve, compensation). They argue that topology enables not only description of pathology but predictive models of spread and functional consequences.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a high-level review of mostly macroscopic clinical connectomics, not a nanoscale EM wiring diagram. No specific diseases, datasets, or model accuracies appear in the abstract. Predictive-model language is programmatic.

plain_language_summary: Brain diseases often travel along the brain’s existing roads rather than staying in one neighborhood. This review explains how mapping those roads can help predict where damage will spread and how the brain copes.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy is then the only method with resolution to identify and follow every axon and dendrite in dense neuropil, which is required for local circuit reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing even local circuits meant serially sectioning and tracing thousands of sections, a daunting manual bottleneck that blocked large volumes.
ocar.action: Briggman and Denk, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2006), review volume electron microscopy developments that improve data quality and automate acquisition.
ocar.resolution: They argue these advances open the prospect of reconstructing almost complete invertebrate nervous systems and sizable fractions of vertebrate ones, and could revive relating function to neuroanatomical circuitry.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is complete neural wiring diagrams via automated volume EM; the review itself is a 2006 outlook, not a finished whole-animal connectome.

summaries.beginner: To see every wire in a tangle of brain tissue you need electron microscopy, but cutting and tracing thousands of slices used to be crushing work. This 2006 review describes machines that collect those 3D pictures more automatically.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2006), K. Briggman and W. Denk review volume EM for neural circuit reconstruction. They note that only EM then had resolution to follow every process in dense neuropil, but serial-section labor blocked large volumes. Improved quality and automated acquisition, they argue, make almost complete invertebrate reconstructions and sizable vertebrate fractions realistic, potentially linking function back to wiring.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Historical outlook from 2006; it does not report a completed connectome or name a specific automated instrument with throughput numbers. “Almost complete invertebrate” is a prospect, not a result in this abstract.

plain_language_summary: To see every wire in a tangle of brain tissue you need electron microscopy, but cutting and tracing thousands of slices used to be crushing work. This 2006 review describes machines that collect those 3D pictures more automatically.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has an invariant cell lineage, a tractable neuron count, and synaptic reconstructions across development, so one can ask how wiring is built from birth to adulthood in graph terms.
ocar.challenge: Static graph models miss the time order of cell divisions and synapse change. Lineage events and connectome snapshots are different kinds of dynamic graphs and are easy to analyze in isolation.
ocar.action: Gayen and Alicea introduce DevoTG on arXiv (2026): Temporal Graph Neural Networks on a continuous-time dynamic graph of lineage divisions and a discrete-time dynamic graph of eight EM connectome reconstructions from L1 to adult.
ocar.resolution: On lineage prediction the TGN reached mean test AUC 0.839 ± 0.007 (5 seeds; validation 0.937 ± 0.001), 26 AUC points above a static GNN with the same architecture (0.577 ± 0.080). On the connectome graph they assign connections among 225 neurons (858 to 2,496 edges over development) to stable, developmental, and variable classes, and they report persistent, strengthening hub roles for command interneurons AVA, AVB, and AVE. Code and visualizations are released.
ocar.future_work: Limitations in the paper include training the TGN on lineage rather than synapse formation, a fixed 6-of-8 timepoint threshold for “stable” edges, treating gap junctions like chemical synapses, and restriction to C. elegans; they flag training on the connectome dynamic graph and cross-species tests as next steps.

summaries.beginner: Roundworms build their tiny brains in a fixed sequence of cell divisions and then keep rewiring synapses as they grow. This software treats that story as a movie of graphs so a computer can learn what happens next and which connections stay put.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2026), Jayadratha Gayen and Bradly Alicea present DevoTG, applying temporal graph neural networks to C. elegans development. A continuous-time graph encodes lineage divisions; a discrete-time graph encodes eight EM connectomes from L1 to adult (225 neurons; 858–2,496 connections). The TGN’s lineage-prediction test AUC is 0.839 ± 0.007 versus 0.577 ± 0.080 for a matched static GNN. Connectome analysis yields stable, developmental, and variable edge classes (complementing Witvliet et al.) and tracks hub command interneurons AVA, AVB, and AVE. Interactive visualizations and code are public.
summaries.advanced: The strong AUC comparison is for cell-division prediction, not synapse-time prediction; the authors say training on the connectome dynamic graph remains future work. Stability uses a fixed 6/8 snapshot threshold whose sensitivity is not fully mapped here. Gap junctions are pooled with chemical synapses. Hub analysis is descriptive centrality, not a causal perturbation. The extract does not support claims about other species. Catalog year and arXiv id match a 2026 preprint.

plain_language_summary: Roundworms build their tiny brains in a fixed sequence of cell divisions and then keep rewiring synapses as they grow. This software treats that story as a movie of graphs so a computer can learn what happens next and which connections stay put.

ocar.opportunity: Segmenting 3D nuclei is basic to counting cells, reading expression, and following lineages, but neuronal-nuclei benchmarks were tiny: volumes below 10⁻³ mm³ and fewer than 500 instances, too small for regional complexity.
ocar.challenge: At sub-cubic-millimeter scale, nuclei vary widely in appearance and density across imaging modalities, and prior 3D methods miss combinations of foreground, contour, and distance cues needed for high-quality instance masks.
ocar.action: Lin, Wei, Petkova, Lichtman, Pfister and colleagues, at MICCAI (2021), release NucMM: a 0.1 mm³ EM volume of nearly an entire zebrafish brain (~170,000 nuclei) and a 0.25 mm³ micro-CT volume of mouse visual cortex (~7,000 nuclei). They train U3D-BCD, a hybrid model using foreground mask, contour map, and signed distance transform.
ocar.resolution: Benchmarks on NucMM show U3D-BCD outperforming prior nuclei-segmentation approaches by a relative 22% in overall score and ranking first on 6 of 7 reported scores. Decoding-parameter checks on validation data suggest signed-distance thresholds matter more than seed foreground/contour thresholds. Code and data are posted.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the dense annotations to support uses beyond the original task, including feature pre-training, shape analysis, and benchmarks for active learning and domain adaptation.

summaries.beginner: Counting brain-cell nuclei in 3D pictures gets hard when the chunk of tissue is large and crowded. This team releases two big labeled volumes—a fish brain and a bit of mouse cortex—and a computer method that outlines those nuclei more cleanly than earlier tools in their tests.
summaries.intermediate: At MICCAI (2021), Lin, Wei, Petkova, Wu, Ahmed, Lichtman, Pfister and colleagues introduce NucMM: ~170,000 nuclei in 0.1 mm³ zebrafish-brain EM and ~7,000 nuclei in 0.25 mm³ mouse visual-cortex micro-CT, both fully annotated. They propose U3D-BCD, combining foreground, contour, and signed-distance representations. On held-out test data (90% of each volume after validation tuning) the model beats prior methods by a relative 22% overall and ranks first in 6 of 7 scores. Code and data are at the Connectomics Bazaar NucMM site.
summaries.advanced: This is nuclei instance segmentation, not synapse or neurite reconstruction; do not read it as a zebrafish or MICrONS connectome. “Nearly the entire zebrafish brain” refers to the 0.1 mm³ EM volume’s coverage claim, not a synaptic wiring diagram. The 22% figure is a relative overall score across two volumes, not a universal AP. Individual AP table cells in the extract are fragmented and should not be quoted out of context. Catalog dataset tags that mention MICrONS are not supported as this paper’s mouse source in the PDF (the volume is described as micro-CT of part of visual cortex).

plain_language_summary: Counting brain-cell nuclei in 3D pictures gets hard when the chunk of tissue is large and crowded. This team releases two big labeled volumes—a fish brain and a bit of mouse cortex—and a computer method that outlines those nuclei more cleanly than earlier tools in their tests.

ocar.opportunity: Human brains are huge, complex, and mostly off-limits to invasive experiments, so neuroscience depends on model organisms. Adding the smallest insects could cut cost and speed circuit mapping.
ocar.challenge: Even standard insect and vertebrate models remain expensive to map completely. Miniature insects are comparable in body size to unicellular organisms yet keep complex brains, so they are easy to overlook as connectomic models.
ocar.action: Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), argue for miniature insects alongside macaque, mouse, zebrafish, fly, and nematode models.
ocar.resolution: They note that the smallest insects still have brains with thousands of neurons, retain insect advantages of identifiable neurons and stereotyped connectomes, yet are smaller and thus easier to map. Their brains also offer evolutionary insight into compact brain design.
ocar.future_work: The review proposes adding these animals to the model-organism toolkit; it does not present a new miniature-insect connectome.

summaries.beginner: Some insects are almost as small as a single cell but still have brains with thousands of neurons. This essay says mapping those tiny brains could teach us how nervous systems stay capable when space is extremely tight.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Makarova, Polilov, and Chklovskii propose miniature insects as connectomic models. Despite body sizes comparable to unicellular organisms, these insects retain complex brains (thousands of neurons) with neuronal identifiability and connectome stereotypy, while being smaller—and therefore easier to map—than conventional insect brains. The authors also highlight evolutionary lessons for compact brain design.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No species list, neuron counts beyond “thousands,” or new reconstructions appear in the abstract. Catalog dataset tags (C. elegans, zebrafish) and organism “fly” are collection metadata, not results of this review.

plain_language_summary: Some insects are almost as small as a single cell but still have brains with thousands of neurons. This essay says mapping those tiny brains could teach us how nervous systems stay capable when space is extremely tight.

ocar.opportunity: An anterior brain was central to early bilaterian success. Relating today’s brains to that ancestral core needs a laboratory animal with both a full connectome and a cellular gene-expression atlas.
ocar.challenge: What core circuits the first bilaterian brain contained, and how they map onto living diversity, is still unsettled without jointly anatomical and molecular maps in a slowly evolving marine invertebrate.
ocar.action: Arendt, Quintana Urzainqui, and Vergara, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), synthesize two Platynereis dumerilii larva resources—the full connectome and a multimodal cellular atlas of gene expression and ultrastructure.
ocar.resolution: The data suggest a composite ancestral bilaterian brain: the anterior end of a circular CNS fused to a sensory-neurosecretory apical system, with lhx6-arx-dlx chemosensory circuits giving rise to associative centers in descendant lineages.
ocar.future_work: The review places the young Platynereis worm at the center of comparative bilaterian neuroanatomy; further phylogenetic tests are implied rather than executed here.

summaries.beginner: To guess what the first complex-animal brain looked like, scientists need a simple marine worm that still has an old-fashioned layout. This review uses a complete wiring map plus gene labels in young Platynereis worms to sketch that ancestral core.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), D. Arendt, Idoia Quintana Urzainqui, and H. Vergara review the Platynereis dumerilii larval full connectome and a multimodal cellular atlas combining gene expression and ultrastructure. They argue for a composite ancestral bilaterian brain: anterior circular CNS fused to a sensory-neurosecretory apical nervous system, with lhx6-arx-dlx chemosensory circuits as precursors of associative centers.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a comparative review of landmark Platynereis resources, not a new connectome in this article. Ancestral reconstructions are evolutionary inferences, not direct fossils. Gene names (lhx6, arx, dlx) are markers in the argument, not quantified expression tables here.

plain_language_summary: To guess what the first complex-animal brain looked like, scientists need a simple marine worm that still has an old-fashioned layout. This review uses a complete wiring map plus gene labels in young Platynereis worms to sketch that ancestral core.

ocar.opportunity: Pairing neuroimaging with genetically informative designs can link molecules to how human structural and functional connectomes are organized.
ocar.challenge: Genetic effects on connectivity are studied with several designs that have different strengths, and it is unclear how they converge on which connections are most heritable.
ocar.action: Arnatkevic̆iūtė, Fulcher, Bellgrove, and Fornito review this interface in NeuroImage (2021), covering twin heritability, DNA-variant association studies, and spatial coupling of imaging phenotypes to transcriptional atlases.
ocar.resolution: They report converging evidence that anatomical connectivity is under stronger genetic influence than functional connectivity, and that genetic influence is uneven across regions and connections. They also discuss using imaging genetics to study how genes contribute to clinical brain dysfunction.
ocar.future_work: The review treats combining imaging and genetics as a route into disordered connectomes; it does not present a new GWAS.

summaries.beginner: Some of the way your brain is wired is written in DNA, but not every connection is equally genetic. This review explains three ways scientists measure that, from twins to gene-expression maps.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2021), Arnatkevic̆iūtė, Fulcher, Bellgrove, and Fornito review genetic bases of human brain networks via twin heritability, association studies of DNA variants, and alignment of imaging phenotypes with transcriptional atlases. They emphasize foundations, strengths, limits, and findings of each. Converging evidence in the review is that structural connectivity is under stronger genetic control than functional connectivity, with spatially non-uniform effects, and that imaging genetics can inform clinical disorders.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Review-level conclusions; the abstract gives no heritability coefficients, loci, or sample sizes. The catalog DOI is an OSF preprint identifier even though the venue is listed as NeuroImage. This is human MRI-scale connectomics, not synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: Some of the way your brain is wired is written in DNA, but not every connection is equally genetic. This review explains three ways scientists measure that, from twins to gene-expression maps.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans was mapped at genes, cells, and synapses early, becoming the first metazoan with a complete cell lineage, sequenced genome, and connectome, and it remains a booming neurodevelopment system.
ocar.challenge: Telling a coherent story from those classic maps to current work on diversification, navigation, connectivity, glia, sexual dimorphism, and plasticity requires a perspective that still points to open questions.
ocar.action: Georgia Rapti, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), reviews C. elegans neurodevelopment from Brenner, Sulston and colleagues through contemporary mechanisms.
ocar.resolution: The perspective summarizes how neural components are generated and diversified, how processes navigate and connect, and highlights recent work on glia, sex dimorphism, and developmental plasticity, arguing that multi-level model-organism studies still expand mechanistic understanding.
ocar.future_work: Rapti frames emerging questions for future discoveries while connecting current research back to the pioneering lineage and connectome work.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm C. elegans was the first animal with a complete cell-by-cell birth record and a full wiring diagram. This perspective walks from those classic maps to newer work on how its nervous system is built, including glia and differences between the sexes.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), Georgia Rapti reviews C. elegans neurodevelopment from early lineage and connectome mapping to current molecular and cellular studies. She covers generation and diversification of neural components, axon navigation and connectivity, and recent emphasis on glia, sexual dimorphism, and plasticity, tying modern results back to Brenner, Sulston and colleagues.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a perspective review, not a new connectome or lineage table. No primary measurements appear in the abstract. Catalog dataset DS01 is collection metadata, not a result reported here.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm C. elegans was the first animal with a complete cell-by-cell birth record and a full wiring diagram. This perspective walks from those classic maps to newer work on how its nervous system is built, including glia and differences between the sexes.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain dynamics in a vertebrate need a cellular map of shapes and projections. Larval zebrafish at 6 days post-fertilization are small enough for brain-wide light microscopy, and a catalog of cell shapes can also serve as ground truth for later synapse-scale EM tracing.
ocar.challenge: Larval zebrafish neuroanatomy was relatively uncharted at whole-brain cellular resolution. Synapse-scale EM is not always required for organizational questions, but mesoscale wiring still needs registered morphologies, genetic expression patterns, and a regional parcellation.
ocar.action: Kunst, Laurell, Mokayes, Kramer, Kubo, Fernandes, Förster, Dal Maschio, and Baier, in Neuron (2019), reconstruct over 2,000 individually GFP-labeled neurons, cluster them into morphotypes, co-register over 100 transgene patterns, and annotate 72 non-overlapping brain regions to build an inter-areal wiring diagram, including virtual tract tracing in tectum and cerebellum.
ocar.resolution: They report a digital atlas with many previously unknown morphologies, hierarchical NBLAST clustering that recovers known classes and suggests novel ones, and previously unknown wiring principles in tectum and cerebellum (including layered retinal versus non-retinal tectal input and thalamic and contralateral MON contributions). They present the resource as the first brain-wide single-cell-resolution inter-areal wiring diagram in a vertebrate, as an evolving open computational tool.
ocar.future_work: The discussion envisions an open repository akin to NeuroMorpho, and argues that a full cell-type census will likely need gene-expression profiling, with morphological classes ideally joined to transcriptional profiles and developmental lineages.

summaries.beginner: A week-old zebrafish is small enough that researchers can trace thousands of single brain cells in the living animal. This atlas turns those shapes into a clickable map of who projects where, including some wiring rules in vision and motor centers that were not obvious before.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2019), Kunst, Laurell, Mokayes, Kramer, Kubo, Fernandes, Förster, Dal Maschio, and Baier present a 6 dpf larval zebrafish atlas based on reconstructions of over 2,000 GFP-labeled neurons, clustered into morphotypes with spatial coordinates. Over 100 transgene patterns are co-registered. Annotating 72 non-overlapping regions yields a mesoscale inter-areal wiring diagram used as ground truth for EM efforts. Virtual tract tracing reports new tectal and cerebellar organization, including non-retinal tectal inputs (notably thalamus and contralateral MON). The authors frame it as a first vertebrate brain-wide cellular wiring diagram.
summaries.advanced: This is light-microscopy mesoscale connectivity from sparsely labeled neurons, not a synapse-resolved EM connectome of the whole larva. “Over 2,000” is not a complete census. NBLAST clustering is noted to overweight soma and neurite location versus intrinsic shape, so novel morphotypes need cautious interpretation. A figure legend in the extract says 36 regions were manually defined while the abstract uses 72; the extract does not reconcile that count. Catalog dataset tags that include Drosophila larva are not supported by this zebrafish PDF.

plain_language_summary: A week-old zebrafish is small enough that researchers can trace thousands of single brain cells in the living animal. This atlas turns those shapes into a clickable map of who projects where, including some wiring rules in vision and motor centers that were not obvious before.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila is a key neurobiology model, but systems-level function is limited without a brain-wide neuron-level network map.
ocar.challenge: Building that map from single-neuron images and then reading community structure, centrality, and small-world or rich-club organization requires a large registered morphology collection.
ocar.action: Shih, Lin, Wang, Chen, Su, Lo, Chiang and colleagues, in Neuroinformatics (2019), build a neuron-to-neuron network from 28,573 single-neuron fluorescence images in FlyCircuit v1.2 and run modularity and centrality analyses.
ocar.resolution: They identify eight communities (right and left olfaction, olfactory core, auditory, motor, pre-motor, left and right vision). Different functional communities dominate different centrality types. Except for the two olfaction communities and the motor community, the network shows overall small-worldness. A rich club is present, with innermost members mostly innervating the central complex. They also report many loops shorter than seven neurons.
ocar.future_work: The abstract treats these motifs as characterizing information processing in the fly brain; further physiological tests are not described here.

summaries.beginner: If you photograph tens of thousands of single fruit-fly neurons, you can sketch a whole-brain social network of cells. This study finds eight neighborhoods—smell, vision, hearing, movement—and a richly connected club in the central complex.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroinformatics (2019), Shih, Lin, Wang, Chen, Su, Lo, Chiang and colleagues construct a neuron-to-neuron Drosophila network from 28,573 FlyCircuit v1.2 single-neuron images. Modularity analysis yields eight communities (bilateral olfaction, olfactory core, auditory, motor, pre-motor, bilateral vision). Centrality type differs by community function. Small-worldness holds except in the two olfactory communities and the motor community. A rich club is reported, with innermost members innervating the central complex, plus numerous loops of length less than seven.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a fluorescence-morphology network from FlyCircuit, not an EM synapse connectome; “connections” are inferred innervation overlaps as used in that resource, which the abstract does not re-specify. Community names are functional interpretations. No modularity Q, rich-club coefficients, or small-world sigma values appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: If you photograph tens of thousands of single fruit-fly neurons, you can sketch a whole-brain social network of cells. This study finds eight neighborhoods—smell, vision, hearing, movement—and a richly connected club in the central complex.

ocar.opportunity: Platynereis dumerilii larvae are small and transparent, so whole-body cell-type and circuit analyses are feasible in an invertebrate with biology missing from C. elegans and Drosophila.
ocar.challenge: Cataloguing neuronal types in this annelid, and relating them to circuits and to cell types absent from major invertebrate models, needs a synthesis of atlases, single-cell RNA-seq, and serial EM.
ocar.action: Williams and Jékely review neuronal cell types in Platynereis in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), covering gene-expression atlases, scRNA-seq, whole-body serial-EM connectomics, and experimental circuit work.
ocar.resolution: They summarize identified types and functions and stress features absent from worm and fly models, including ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptors.
ocar.future_work: The review positions Platynereis as a laboratory model bridging cell-type diversity and circuits; further type-to-synapse inventories are implied.

summaries.beginner: A small marine worm larva is clear enough to list its brain-cell types in the whole body. This review explains those cell types and notes extras that fruit flies and soil worms do not have, such as cilia-based swimming sensors.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Elizabeth A. Williams and G. Jékely review neuronal cell types in Platynereis dumerilii. Approaches include whole-body gene-expression atlases, single-cell RNA-seq, serial-EM connectomics, and functional experiments. They highlight biology missing from C. elegans and Drosophila: ciliary locomotion, noradrenergic neurons, and ciliary photoreceptors.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Review of an emerging model, not a new complete synapse list in this article. No cell-type counts or scRNA-seq cluster numbers appear in the abstract. Catalog co-tagging of C. elegans marks comparison, not a worm dataset produced here.

plain_language_summary: A small marine worm larva is clear enough to list its brain-cell types in the whole body. This review explains those cell types and notes extras that fruit flies and soil worms do not have, such as cilia-based swimming sensors.

ocar.opportunity: Light and electron microscopy, plus better handling of large datasets, are starting to contribute connectomes in multiple organisms—maps of how neurons and regions connect.
ocar.challenge: Acquisition and analysis of connectomic data remain hard. Macroscopic and mesoscopic maps already look complicated; EM-scale maps show unimaginable synaptic complexity. Handling and automated analysis still need substantial improvement.
ocar.action: Ohno, Katoh, Y. Saitoh, and S. Saitoh review these challenges in Microscopy (2016), covering imaging modalities and the complexity revealed at macroscopic, mesoscopic, and microscopic scales.
ocar.resolution: They describe unidirectional and reciprocal cortical networks at coarser scales and extreme synaptic complexity at EM scale, and they argue that multidisciplinary combinations of imaging modalities, plus automation, are needed to ask whether a complete connectome can explain basic and higher human brain functions.
ocar.future_work: The review calls for efficient dataset handling, automated analyses, and multimodal combination as the path toward structural and functional connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Making a full wiring diagram of a brain means collecting enormous pictures and then making sense of them. This 2016 review surveys how light and electron microscopes are doing that, and why the data are still almost too big to handle.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy (2016), N. Ohno, Mitsuhiko Katoh, Y. Saitoh, and S. Saitoh review imaging contributions to connectomics and the data-analysis bottleneck. They contrast macroscopic and light-microscopic (“mesoscopic”) maps of uni- and reciprocal cortical connections with electron-microscopic (“microscopic”) synaptic complexity. They emphasize innovation in acquisition and analysis and argue that combining modalities will be needed to test whether complete connectomes explain brain function, including in humans.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Historical review; no new volume, species, or accuracy numbers. Human-function language is a closing question, not a result. Scale labels (macro/meso/micro) are the authors’ usage.

plain_language_summary: Making a full wiring diagram of a brain means collecting enormous pictures and then making sense of them. This 2016 review surveys how light and electron microscopes are doing that, and why the data are still almost too big to handle.

ocar.opportunity: New volume-EM hardware and specimen methods let researchers see cells in 3D with unprecedented detail, reviving ultrastructural cell biology beyond specialized serial-section labs.
ocar.challenge: Serial-section techniques were historically specialist crafts. Broad biomedical use needed automation (tape-collecting ultramicrotomes, serial block-face and focused-ion-beam SEMs) and ways to combine light and electron data without tedious specimen transfers.
ocar.action: Peddie and Collinson review this coming-of-age in Micron (2014), covering automated serial methods, pending microscope-design innovations, and integrated light-and-electron systems for correlative volume EM.
ocar.resolution: They argue the scope of volume EM is widening beyond the brain, that speed and quality of collection should keep improving, and that integrated CLEM will make sequential light then electron data in the same 3D space routine, linking function to ultrastructure.
ocar.future_work: The review looks ahead to further microscope-design innovations and routine correlative light and volume EM without intermediate specimen manipulation.

summaries.beginner: Three-dimensional electron microscopy used to be a rare craft. This review describes machines that automatically slice and scan tissue, and new setups that take light-microscope and electron-microscope pictures of the same sample.
summaries.intermediate: In Micron (2014), C. Peddie and L. Collinson review volume electron microscopy as it became more automated via ATUM-style tape collection, serial block-face SEM, and FIB-SEM, with applications expanding beyond brain tissue. They discuss forthcoming microscope-design improvements and integrated light-electron systems that would allow correlative volume EM without transferring the specimen between modalities.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Methods review from 2014, not a dataset paper. No voxel sizes, throughputs, or species results are in the abstract. Integrated CLEM is described as upcoming, not as a completed instrument characterization here.

plain_language_summary: Three-dimensional electron microscopy used to be a rare craft. This review describes machines that automatically slice and scan tissue, and new setups that take light-microscope and electron-microscope pictures of the same sample.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic layout inside a circuit is a prime determinant of function. Fine-scale maps of hippocampal CA3–CA1 synapses could show whether connections are random or spatially structured.
ocar.challenge: Seeing individual synapses between identified neurons across that projection required a labeling method dense enough for comprehensive mapping.
ocar.action: Druckmann, Feng, Lee, Yook, Zhao, Magee, and Kim, in Neuron (2014), map CA3–CA1 connectivity with the synapse-labeling method mGRASP.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity is spatially nonuniform and clustered. Clustering is enhanced among neurons that shared a similar developmental or migration time window, suggesting a developmental mechanism for spatial synaptic structure. Such patterns are discussed as potentially engaging active dendritic computation and storage and enhancing feature selectivity.
ocar.future_work: The abstract links clustered structure to dendritic processing and selectivity; further causal tests of that link are not reported here.

summaries.beginner: In hippocampus, connections are not sprinkled at random. This paper labels individual synapses between two regions and finds they come in clusters, especially among cells born around the same time.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2014), Druckmann, Feng, Lee, Yook, Zhao, Magee, and Kim use mGRASP for fine-scale mapping of hippocampal CA3–CA1 synapses. They report spatially nonuniform, clustered connectivity, stronger among neurons with similar developmental or migration timing. They suggest this structure could engage active dendritic processing and storage and enhance neuronal feature selectivity.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract gives no synapse counts, cluster statistics, or animal numbers. Feature-selectivity language is interpretive (“thought to”). mGRASP reports labeled contacts, not a full EM-verified CA1 connectome.

plain_language_summary: In hippocampus, connections are not sprinkled at random. This paper labels individual synapses between two regions and finds they come in clusters, especially among cells born around the same time.

ocar.opportunity: High-quality 3D reconstructions of axons and dendrites revived the hope of inferring synaptic connectivity from geometry—“neurogeometry”—without always seeing every synapse.
ocar.challenge: A quantitative theory of that inference needs a clear definition of when an axon and dendrite are close enough to host a synapse.
ocar.action: Stepanyants and Chklovskii review this framework in Trends in Neurosciences (2005), centering the “potential synapse”: a close axo-dendritic apposition needed to form an actual synapse.
ocar.resolution: Neurogeometry then describes potential connectivity in circuits and, they argue, sheds light on functional connectivity features such as specificity and plasticity.
ocar.future_work: The review offers a theoretical framework rather than a new reconstruction; applying potential-synapse statistics to additional circuits is the implied use.

summaries.beginner: If you know the 3D shapes of axons and dendrites, you can guess where they come close enough to form a synapse. This review names those near-misses “potential synapses” and explains why the idea matters for learning and specificity.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2005), A. Stepanyants and D. Chklovskii review neurogeometry: inferring connectivity from axonal and dendritic shapes. They define a potential synapse as a close apposition required to form an actual synapse, and they argue this geometric description informs specificity and plasticity of functional connectivity.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Conceptual review; no measurements, species, or potential-versus-actual conversion rates appear in the abstract. Potential synapses are geometric candidates, not counted EM synapses.

plain_language_summary: If you know the 3D shapes of axons and dendrites, you can guess where they come close enough to form a synapse. This review names those near-misses “potential synapses” and explains why the idea matters for learning and specificity.

ocar.opportunity: Machine-learning networks have an architecture, a loss, and a learning rule. If biology uses a simple excitatory–inhibitory motif to compare inputs to a reference, that motif could supply both a loss-like signal and homeostatic control.
ocar.challenge: Whether such an XOR motif is common in real connectomes, and whether homeostasis alone could drive a relevant form of plasticity, is speculative without counting the motif across species.
ocar.action: Jesus Marco de Lucas, in an arXiv short comment (2024), describes a 4:1 excitatory-to-inhibitory XOR motif that outputs a discrepancy and can halt propagation, links it to winner-take-all patterns, and counts its occurrence in published connectomes from C. elegans through Drosophila neuropils to mouse V1.
ocar.resolution: Motif prevalence is reported as tens in C. elegans, millions in several Drosophila neuropils, and more than tens of millions in mouse V1. If validated, the author argues this identifies architecture and loss in the machine-learning analogy, with plasticity as an evolved regulatory control. A table in the extract also lists layered XOR-like patterns in a 10-million-connection shuffled subset of a cortical connectome.
ocar.future_work: How XOR feedback is reinjected to promote plasticity is unconfirmed; the author is exploring spiking implementations via backpropagation through time with axonal delays, and notes more complex E/I patterns (PV, SOM, VIP) may appear in cortical microcircuit models.

summaries.beginner: Computers learn by measuring how wrong they are. This speculative note asks whether a small mix of “go” and “stop” brain cells could do the same job while keeping activity in balance, and then counts that pattern in worm, fly, and mouse wiring maps.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2024), J. M. D. Lucas (Jesus Marco de Lucas) proposes an XOR motif of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (core 4:1 E:I) that signals mismatch to a reference and supports homeostasis and winner-take-all. Counting the motif in published connectomes, he reports tens in C. elegans, millions in several Drosophila neuropils, and more than tens of millions in mouse V1. The comment is framed as identifying architecture and loss, with learning methods still being explored in spiking nets.
summaries.advanced: This is a brief speculative commentary, not a new reconstruction or a causal plasticity experiment. Motif counts inherit definitions and completeness of the source connectomes; “if validated” is the author’s own hedge. The 4:1 ratio is the proposed core motif, not a measured census of all E/I cells. Fragmentary cortical-layer tables in the extract should not be over-quoted. The extract does not demonstrate that homeostasis is sufficient for learning in vivo.

plain_language_summary: Computers learn by measuring how wrong they are. This speculative note asks whether a small mix of “go” and “stop” brain cells could do the same job while keeping activity in balance, and then counts that pattern in worm, fly, and mouse wiring maps.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM now yields complete neurite wiring maps in large volumes and even entire nervous systems in a growing list of species. Combining that structure with genetic and molecular identity would show how specific neurons and circuits interact.
ocar.challenge: Purely morphological EM often identifies elements only by shape, so genetically or molecularly defined cells are hard to place in the same volume.
ocar.action: Ohno, Karube, and Fujiyama review, in Neuroscience Research (2024), tools that add molecular and gene-expression context to volume EM, including probes visible in EM and correlative methods that match the same objects across light and electron modalities.
ocar.resolution: They argue these advances can clarify interactions of specific neurons and circuits and may illuminate basal-ganglia networks involving dopamine neurons, toward mechanisms of adaptive change in defined circuits.
ocar.future_work: The review expects such multimodal EM to reveal how specific circuits modulate brain function; it does not itself present a new genetically identified volume.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope maps show every branch but often not which genetic type a cell is. This review covers new stains and matching tricks that let researchers see defined cell types in those 3D maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience Research (2024), Nobuhiko Ohno, F. Karube, and Fumino Fujiyama review volume EM for genetically and molecularly defined circuits. They contrast complete wiring maps now available in several species with the limits of morphology-only identification, then survey EM-visible probes and correlative multi-modal registration. They suggest applications to specific circuits, including basal-ganglia networks with dopamine neurons, and to adaptive behavioral change.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Methods review; no new volume or dopamine-circuit reconstruction is reported in the abstract. Basal-ganglia language is prospective (“may help to elucidate”). Do not treat this card as a completed genetically labeled connectome.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope maps show every branch but often not which genetic type a cell is. This review covers new stains and matching tricks that let researchers see defined cell types in those 3D maps.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic wiring diagrams could tightly constrain detailed circuit models if connectivity could be related to physiological properties.
ocar.challenge: Turning a connectome into physiology is still difficult: synapse counts do not automatically yield weights, signs, or dynamics.
ocar.action: Ganguly and Litwin-Kumar, in a Current Biology (2022) dispatch, discuss a new study of that relationship in a fruit-fly neural pathway.
ocar.resolution: They present the commented study as describing how connectivity relates to physiology in that pathway and as suggesting a path forward for future models. The catalog abstract does not name the study’s quantitative findings.
ocar.future_work: The dispatch points to that fly pathway result as a template for future connectome-constrained models.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is not yet a working model of a brain circuit. This short commentary highlights a fruit-fly study that tries to match synapses to how cells actually fire, as a clue for building better models.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Ishani Ganguly and Ashok Litwin-Kumar write a dispatch on relating connectomes to physiology. They note that wiring diagrams promise constraints for detailed models but that linking connectivity to physiological properties is challenging, and they highlight a new fruit-fly pathway study as describing that relationship and suggesting a modeling path forward.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a commentary, not the primary fly study. The abstract does not name the pathway, neurons, or any physiological measurements, so this card cannot report those results. Do not invent accuracies or synapse counts.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is not yet a working model of a brain circuit. This short commentary highlights a fruit-fly study that tries to match synapses to how cells actually fire, as a clue for building better models.

ocar.opportunity: A mechanistic account of human brain function needs how neurons and regions connect across scales, from MRI tractography to axonal and synaptic microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Diffusion MRI and tractography shaped human connectomics but lack the resolution of polarization, fluorescence, or electron microscopy. Whole-brain tractography must be informed and constrained by regional high-resolution data and local fiber geometry, and atlases must represent uncertainty.
ocar.action: Axer and Amunts, in Science (2022), review this nested human connectome and the methods required to join scales.
ocar.resolution: They argue new methods must constrain tractography with regional microscopy and local geometry; machine learning and simulation can predict missing experimental data; future interoperable atlases need high-resolution templates and directionality to represent alternative tractography solutions and accuracy estimates.
ocar.future_work: The review’s program is nested, interoperable multi-scale human atlases that carry directionality and uncertainty, not a single new dataset in this article.

summaries.beginner: Human brain maps from MRI see big cables; microscopes see single axons. This Science piece argues we need both, nested together, and honest estimates of how wrong the big-scale maps might be.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2022), M. Axer and K. Amunts review the nested human connectome across MRI tractography and microscopic methods (polarization, fluorescence, electron microscopy). They call for constraining whole-brain tractography with regional high-resolution connectivity and local fiber geometry, using machine learning and simulation where data are missing, and building interoperable atlases with high-resolution templates, directionality, and estimates of tractography accuracy.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Perspective/review; no new human EM volume or tractography benchmark numbers appear in the abstract. Machine-learning “predictions where data are missing” is a proposed need, not a validated algorithm here.

plain_language_summary: Human brain maps from MRI see big cables; microscopes see single axons. This Science piece argues we need both, nested together, and honest estimates of how wrong the big-scale maps might be.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic weight matrices shape network function, but many networks can implement similar responses and the same network can behave differently by context. Geometry might reveal which connections are actually required by a set of responses.
ocar.challenge: Quantitative structure–function links are subtle. It is largely unknown whether particular synapses must exist to generate specified network-level computations, especially in recurrent circuits.
ocar.action: Biswas and Fitzgerald, in Physical Review Research (2022; arXiv 2020), introduce a geometric framework for threshold-linear recurrent networks. When the number of specified steady-state response patterns does not exceed the number of input synapses, they analytically compute the space of feedforward and recurrent connectivity matrices consistent with those responses, including a noisy generalization.
ocar.resolution: The solution-space geometry can undergo topological transitions as allowed error grows. From that geometry they derive certainty conditions that guarantee a nonzero synapse between neurons. The framework is offered as a way to turn activity data into anatomical predictions that follow from the model class.
ocar.future_work: The authors state the theory could be applied to neural activity data to make rigorous anatomical predictions; the extracted text does not report such an empirical application.

summaries.beginner: Many different wiring diagrams can make a neural network do the same job, so seeing activity does not uniquely reveal every synapse. This theory paper maps the whole family of wiring diagrams that fit a set of responses, and finds when a connection simply must be there.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review Research (2022; arXiv 2020), Tirthabir Biswas and James E. Fitzgerald analyze recurrent threshold-linear networks. Under the assumption that specified steady-state response patterns do not outnumber input synapses, they calculate the solution space of feedforward and recurrent weights that realize those responses from given inputs. With noise, that space can change topology as error tolerance increases. They derive conditions guaranteeing a nonzero synapse and propose applying the geometry to activity data for anatomical predictions.
summaries.advanced: This is an analytical theory paper for a specific architecture (threshold-linear, steady-state responses, pattern count ≤ input synapses). The PDF extract is dominated by the abstract, introduction, and bibliography; it does not include a worked biological dataset or synapse-call accuracies. Topological transitions are a predicted geometric phenomenon versus allowed error, not an experimental observation here. Catalog year 2020 is the preprint; the DOI is the 2022 journal article.
